Administered challenges over the last seven years of the competition can be grouped into four core themes: building envelopes, energy management, indoor environmental quality, and technology adoption. The prompts are technical in nature but require holistic solutions that address specific stakeholder needs, incorporate cost/benefit and market analysis, and capture technology-to- market opportunities and barriers. 2.1 Envelope A building envelope is the physical barrier (e.g., walls, roof, windows) separating a building’s interior from the exterior. Advances in envelope materials and construction methods are crucial for energy efficiency and cost improvements. 2.1.1 Pushing the Envelope With Wall Retrofits 2.1.1.1 Objective This challenge focuses on developing innovative solutions for building envelope wall retrofits. 2.1.1.2 Background Building envelopes separate conditioned indoor spaces from outdoor environments and shelter building occupants from weather, sunlight, and noise. The building envelope includes the building’s foundation, walls, roof, ceiling, windows, and items inside these building elements, such as insulation. The envelope serves as a means to support the structure and control the transfer of heat, light, and air between the inside and outside, while being aesthetically pleasing. However, many building envelopes are not tightly sealed, allowing uncontrolled and unwanted air exchange between indoor and outdoor environments. Poor envelopes allow conditioned air to “escape” to the outside (exfiltration) and unconditioned air to enter (infiltration). These airflows increase the total amount of air that needs to be heated or cooled in the building. Improving the building envelope reduces the need for heating and cooling, in turn saving energy and money for the owner or occupants of the building. Insulation in walls and ceilings also helps reduce the heating and cooling needs of buildings by preventing energy loss (from heat transfer) through the building envelope. Many homes do not have insulation because they were built before insulation requirements were in place. Residences can have energy bills that equal 20%–30% of total annual household income, much higher than the 6% considered affordable by economists (Boyce and Wirfs-Brock 2016; Chandler 2016; Shahyd 2016). High energy costs can limit the amount of money American families have for basic necessities. Building envelopes can also become health hazards to occupants if they contain asbestos, lead paint, mold, or mildew. Public health entities have enacted laws and guidelines for the abatement of asbestos and lead paints. Mold spores can detach from these surfaces and reenter the building. Among other consequences, mold has been shown to contribute to the development of asthma in children (Fields 2012). Solutions are needed that allow the existing building envelope to be retrofitted (i.e., updated) to make walls more energy-efficient, air-tight, and moisture-resistant—and therefore healthier.
